title: Your Night Has Grown Long at al-Athmud
intro: Who made this poem is disputed. It stands in every recension of the diwan of Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr that its editor collated, al-Mufaddal's among them; Ibn al-Kalbi gave it to Amr ibn Madikarib, who he said composed it after killing men of Banu Mazin in revenge for his brother Abdallah; and Ibn Durayd gave it to Imru' al-Qays ibn Abis of Kinda, a Companion of the Prophet, the view al-Ayni preferred and al-Zirikli followed. It opens on a sleepless night over news from one Abu al-Aswad, whom the poet will not answer as he would answer anyone else, and turns into a warning to a clan seeking blood: leave the feud buried and so will we, start a war and we will not stay at home. Then come a boast of spearmanship and hospitality and an inventory of his war gear: mare, mail coat, lance and sword. Rhetoricians made the opening famous: al-Zamakhshari wrote that “Imru' al-Qays turned three times in three lines”, moving from “you” to “he” to “I”, and Ibn al-Mu'tazz opened his chapter on fine similes with the two lines on the mail coat, saying “we begin with the leader of the poets.”

translation: Your night has stretched out long at al-Athmud;
the carefree have slept, and you have not.
1.sharh: He speaks to himself: the night drags on, everyone without a care is asleep, and he alone lies awake. Saying “your night” for “my night” is the first of the three shifts of person that rhetoricians admire in these opening lines.

translation: He spent the night, and a night was spent with him
like the night of a man whose eye is sore and inflamed.
2.sharh: Now he talks of himself as “he”: he lay awake through a night as long as that of a man whose eye smarts with grit or inflammation and will not close. This is the second shift of person.

translation: That comes of news that reached me,
that I was told of Abu al-Aswad.
3.sharh: Back in the first person, he gives the cause of his sleeplessness: news he was told on Abu al-Aswad's authority. Having called himself “you”, then “he”, then “I”, he has used all three persons in three lines. Al-Ayni took the news to be of Abu al-Aswad's death.

translation: Had it come to me from another man's talk,
and the tongue wounds as the hand wounds,
4.sharh: Had the words come from anyone but Abu al-Aswad he would not have let them pass, for a wound dealt by the tongue cuts as deep as one dealt by the sword hand. The second half became a proverb about the harm that slander does.

translation: I would have spoken words that would go on
being told of me till the end of time.
5.sharh: He would have answered with satire that people would repeat for ever; only because the news came from Abu al-Aswad does he hold his tongue. The word for “go on” is split between the two halves of the line.

translation: Which of our dealings do you spurn:
Amr's blood, given for Marthad?
6.sharh: He asks a clan still bent on revenge which part of the reckoning they reject, whether it is the blood of Amr, of his own house, given for their Marthad. Amr, he means, was Marthad's equal. Al-Qali reports that neither al-Asma'i nor Abu Amr knew what the first half meant.

translation: If you bury the sickness, we will not bring it out;
if you rouse war, we will not sit idle.
7.sharh: The “sickness” is the feud between the two sides. If the other clan lets it lie buried, his people will not dig it up; if they start a war, his people will not stay at home.

translation: If you kill us, we will kill you over and over;
if you go after blood, we will go after blood.
8.sharh: Any blow will be repaid many times over: the verb for his clan's killing is in the intensive form, the enemy's in the plain one. Whoever seeks their blood will have his own sought.

translation: How long have we known the spearing of armoured champions,
and praise, and glory, and lordship,
9.sharh: He boasts of his clan: spearing armed champions, and the praise, glory and leadership it brings, have always been theirs. The diwan's commentator takes the question “how long” to mean that these never left them.

translation: and raising domed tents, and filling great bowls,
and the fire, and the firewood stirred to blaze?
10.sharh: The boast turns to hospitality: domed tents raised, huge bowls filled for guests, fires kept burning and stirred high. To the Arabs these were the marks of a generous chief.

translation: I have readied for war a mare that leaps,
generous in her running, urged or left at ease,
11.sharh: From his people he turns to his own gear for war, starting with his mare. She gives her best whether he urges her on or lets her go gently.

translation: swimming, headlong, and her gallop
like the crackle of fire in palm fronds,
12.sharh: She stretches out her forelegs as if swimming and runs headlong, and at full gallop the rush of her going sounds like fire roaring through dry palm fronds. Al-Ayni notes that the likeness is one of sound: the hiss of her running and the crackle of the flames.

translation: and a mail coat, tight-riveted and closely woven,
that folds down small as a file,
13.sharh: His mail coat is so finely made that folded up it is no bigger than a file. Al-Tufi says its folds lie close together like the ridges of a file, an image he knew in no other poet. A poem of Amr ibn Madikarib has the same image: a full mail coat whose folds are like a file.

translation: its sleeves pour down over a man
as a flood pours over hard, flat ground,
14.sharh: Having shown the coat folded, he now shows it worn: long and full, flowing over its wearer like floodwater spreading across hard ground. Abu Hilal al-Askari says the likeness lies in its whiteness and the way it covers the whole body; al-Tufi adds its sheen and suppleness.

translation: and a supple lance, like the rope of a deep well
twisted from the fibre of a bare palm,
15.sharh: His lance is long and straight, and a shake runs through it from butt to point. He likens it to the rope of a very deep well, which must be long and true; al-Tufi says the likeness lies in its straightness and length. The word for “deep well” runs over from one half into the next.

translation: and a grooved sword whose wound runs deep,
that does not bend when it strikes bone.
16.sharh: Last comes his sword, its blade marked with grooves, which sinks deep into what it strikes and does not bend even on bone. The list is complete: mare, mail coat, lance and sword.

1.1.3.head: الأَثمُد
1.1.3.meaning: Al-Athmud: a place. Yaqut spells it Ithmid; elsewhere ithmid is the antimony stone ground for kohl.

1.2.2.head: الخَلِيّ
1.2.2.meaning: Khaliyy: someone free of cares, the opposite of the grieving.

2.2.3.head: العائِر
2.2.3.meaning: A'ir: grit in the eye that makes it water; some say eye inflammation itself.

3.2.1.head: خَبَّرَ
3.2.1.meaning: Was told it. The diwan's main text has wa-unbi'tuhu, with the same meaning; this is al-A'lam's reading.

3.2.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Aswad: the commentaries on the diwan do not say who he was; al-Ayni makes him Zalim ibn Amr, a cousin of the poet. Others read it as “my father, the lordly one”.

4.1.3.meaning: Natha: what is said about a man, good or bad; thana', with the long vowel, is only praise.

5.2.4-5.meaning: “The hand of al-musnad”: for ever. Al-musnad is time.

6.2.3.meaning: Amr: a man of the poet's own family, says the diwan's commentator.

6.2.4-5.meaning: For Marthad: Marthad was a man of the clan he addresses.

7.1.5.head: خَفى
7.1.5.meaning: We bring it out: the verb khafa means to reveal, and akhfa to hide.

9.1.4.head: الكُماة
9.1.4.meaning: Kumat: champions armed from head to foot. The word ends at the start of the second half.

10.1.1.head: بَني
10.1.1.meaning: Bany: the raising of a tent or house, not “sons of”.

10.2.4.head: المُفأَد
10.2.4.meaning: Muf'ad: stirred with the mif'ad, the poker.

11.2.2-3.meaning: “Urging and easing”: mahaththa is from urging a horse on, marwad from letting it go gently.

12.1.3.head: إِحضار
12.1.3.meaning: Ihdar: a gallop, faster than the canter.

12.2.1.head: مَعمَعَة
12.2.1.meaning: Ma'ma'a: the roar of a fire as it catches.

13.1.2.head: السَّكّ
13.1.2.meaning: Sakk: the rivets that close the rings of a mail coat.

13.1.3.head: مَوضونَة
13.1.3.meaning: Mawduna: closely woven, like a plaited saddle girth.

14.2.2.head: الأَتِيّ
14.2.2.meaning: Atiyy: a flood that comes from every side.

15.1.3.head: الجَرور
15.1.3.meaning: Jarur: a very deep well. The word ends at the start of the second half.

15.2.3.head: خُلُب
15.2.3.meaning: Khulub: palm fibre, from which ropes are twisted.

16.1.2.head: شُطَب
16.1.2.meaning: Shutab: the grooves running along a sword blade.
